title: Building an Enterprise Agent Inventory
summary: The five build steps are NIST's CM-8 read for a new asset class, plus the three API calls that actually find agents and the one inventory criterion agents break.
body_markdown:
TL;DR


**Building an agent inventory is reconciliation work, and the control that describes it predates agents entirely.** NIST SP 800-53 CM-8 already asks for an inventory that "accurately reflects the system", includes every component, avoids "duplicate accounting", and sits at whatever granularity you need. CM-8(4) asks for the owner by name. CM-8(3) asks for automated detection of things nobody authorized.


Read that way, the five steps below are not a methodology. They are CM-8 applied to an asset class that ships its own credentials.


The common view is that this is a tooling problem. It is mostly a query problem, and three calls do most of the work:` GET /oauth2PermissionGrants` in Microsoft Graph,` GET /admin/directory/v1/users/{userKey}/tokens` in Google Workspace, and the Recommender API's service-account insights, which flag accounts that "haven't authenticated in the past 90 days".


One criterion agents genuinely break, and it is the first one. A record cannot accurately reflect what an agent can do, because under MCP a server's tool set "MAY vary by the authorization presented on the request". Capability is evaluated per call, so the inventory stores a claim about capability rather than capability itself.


Start with the grants. Normalize thin, name an owner, record verbs rather than connections, and tag lifecycle state at discovery time so nothing arrives untagged.
